title: Concomitant multiple subretinal cysticerci in neurocysticercosis
case_text:
A 42-year-old Indian male presented to the emergency services of our institute with an alleged history of a road traffic accident. On examination, the patient's Glasgow Coma scoring was E2V3M4. The patient was intubated. Noncontrast computed tomography revealed multiple well-defined cystic lesions in the cortical and juxtacortical regions. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed multiple ring lesions with enhancing protoscolex which was suggestive of neurocysticercosis (NCC) [Figure 1]. The optic nerve was free of any cysts. An ophthalmology consult was sought before starting anti-helminthic drugs. The anterior segment examination was unremarkable, and pupils were reacting normally to light. Fundoscopy showed clear media and discrete yellow-white placoid subretinal lesions nasal to the optic disc and in the macular area of 0.25 1 DD size in the right eye [Figure 2a]. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) scan through the lesion showed a hyperreflective cystic lesion with backscattering [Figure 2b]. B-scan ultrasound showed an anechoic cystic lesion in the coats of the eye with a hyperechoic scolex [Figure 2c]. The classical imaging findings of multiple cysts with scolex on the MRI head are an absolute criterion for diagnosis of definitive NCC. The ocular ultrasound, OCT, and epidemiology further supported the diagnosis of NCC with multiple subretinal cysticerci; however, the patient had no ocular complaint. The parasite appeared to be in the vesicular stage in both locations, and there was no surrounding inflammation.
Identification of serum antibodies with standard enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay techniques was negative which is a validated test with <70% positivity for intraocular cysticercosis. The stool tests for 3 days did not reveal any parasitic disease.
The patient was started on injectable steroids (dexamethasone 6 mg) followed by albendazole 15 mg/kg. The patient was initially followed up for 2 weeks till his discharge from the hospital. There was an improvement in the Glasgow Coma scores during this period. There were no episodes of fever and seizures. However, there was no resolution of the placoid lesions. Transpupillary thermotherapy was done for the persistent subretinal cysts using a large spot-size diode laser 810 nm [Figure 2d]. Chorioretinal scarring was noted at a week's follow-up visit in the retina clinic after laser treatment, and the patient's vision was documented as 20/20 OU. Unfortunately, no subsequent follow-up is available.

   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Neurocysticercosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: neurocysticercosis with concomitant subretinal cysticerci
